screens.title: Interacting with Smart Contracts from the Frontend
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll learn the essential plumbing that lets a JavaScript frontend talk to a Solidity smart contract. You will understand two fundamental pieces of information — the ABI, which describes a contract’s public interface, and the contract address, which locates a deployed instance on the chain. We’ll also cover how a Web3 provider, such as a browser wallet or a remote node service, becomes the bridge between your app and Ethereum. You will see concrete examples using Ethers. js to perform read-only calls that don’t cost gas and to send signed transactions that modify state. Along the way, we’ll highlight common pitfalls: ABI mismatches, network mismatch, and user-rejected transactions, and why proper error handling matters for user trust. By the end you’ll be able to wire up a simple DApp, call a getter, and submit a transaction securely via the user’s wallet. Think about a minimal counter or storage contract — the patterns we cover will apply directly when you build your own frontend to interact with deployed contracts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Overview
Interacting with Smart Contracts from the Frontend
Understand ABI, addresses, providers, read vs write calls, and safe UX for DApp interactions.
In this lesson
Wire your frontend using Ethers.js. Call view functions, send transactions, and handle user wallet flows safely.
Why it matters
A correct ABI and address let your app encode calls and decode results. A provider signs and submits transactions. Get these right to avoid confusing errors.
Explore Key Topics
ABI & Address
Describe and locate a contract so your frontend encodes and targets calls properly.
Providers & Signers
MetaMask injects a provider and a signer. Remote nodes provide read-only access.
Read vs Write
View functions cost no gas; state-modifying functions require signed transactions and gas.
Concept flow
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
ABI
JSON description of functions, events, and types that lets your frontend encode calls and decode results.
Contract Address
Unique on-chain location for the deployed contract instance. Required to target calls.
Provider
The gateway to an Ethereum node. Browser wallets inject a provider and provide a signer for transactions.
Alt text: three concept cards labeled ABI, Contract Address, and Provider showing their role as the minimal connection required between frontend and contract.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify the ABI and contract address necessary for frontend interactions, configure a Web3 provider so your DApp can send requests, call read-only functions to fetch on-chain data, and construct signed transactions to modify state. Each objective combines a practical skill with why it matters. For example, knowing where the contract lives on the chain and having its ABI ensures your frontend encodes calls correctly and decodes results reliably. Configuring a provider matters because it defines whether you can only read data or also sign transactions on behalf of the user. Calling view or pure functions lets you show live on-chain information without costing gas, while constructing transactions requires careful handling of gas estimation and user approval. Finally, you will learn common issues such as network mismatches and user rejections, and how to handle them gracefully. These competencies let you build a responsive, trustworthy DApp experience and avoid common user confusion during wallet interactions.

screens.title: How you'll apply these skills
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives translate into concrete front-end practices. First, always bundle or load the exact ABI that matches your deployed contract; a mismatch will lead to call failures or 'function not found' errors. Second, detect and surface the connected network to prevent users from sending transactions to the wrong chain. Third, treat every state-changing operation as an asynchronous workflow: prompt the user, send the signed transaction, wait for a receipt, then update the UI. Fourth, provide clear error messages for common issues such as user rejection, gas estimation failures, or insufficient funds. For example, when using Ethers. js, you will instantiate a contract with a provider for read-only access and with a signer for transactions. Practicing these patterns ensures your DApp is reliable, transparent, and respectful of user control over signing transactions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Applications
Verified front-end patterns
  • Load the exact ABI produced at compile time and pair it with the deployed address for the network in use.
  • Use a provider for fetching on-chain data and a signer for creating transactions that require authorization.
  • Always await transaction receipts and update state post-confirmation rather than assuming success immediately.
  • Surface clear error states for user rejection, insufficient funds, and gas estimation failures.
Quick checklist
Is the connected wallet on the same network as the contract?
Does the ABI match the deployed contract version?
Are you using a signer for transactions and a provider for reads?
Do you handle user rejection and gas-related errors gracefully?

screens.title: ABI and Contract Address
screens.narratorSegment: The ABI, or Application Binary Interface, is a JSON array that describes a smart contract's public interface: its functions, events, state variables, argument types, and return types. The contract address is a unique on-chain identifier created when a contract is deployed. Together they let your frontend encode the binary payload for a function call and target a specific contract instance on a given network. A concrete example: a compiled SimpleStorage contract exposes a get function and a set function. Your frontend needs the ABI to call get and decode the returned number. It also needs the contract's deployed address so the Ethereum nodes know which contract to execute. A frequent misconception is thinking the ABI alone is sufficient; without the address the ABI has no target, and without the ABI the frontend cannot package calls correctly. Key practical checks include ensuring the ABI version matches the deployed bytecode and that you are using the address for the same network as the provider. Final takeaway: ABI describes how to talk, address tells you where to speak. Ask yourself: do I have both the exact ABI and the correct deployed address before attempting calls?

keyIdea.title: Describe and locate
keyIdea.text: ABI describes the interface; the contract address locates the deployed instance. Both are required for correct encoding and targeting of calls.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › ABI & Address
Definition
ABI is the JSON contract interface. The address is the unique on-chain location.
Example ABI (simplified)
[
  {
    "inputs": [{ "internalType": "uint256", "name": "_num", "type": "uint256" }],
    "name": "set",
    "outputs": [],
    "stateMutability": "nonpayable",
    "type": "function"
  },
  {
    "inputs": [],
    "name": "get",
    "outputs": [{ "internalType": "uint256", "name": "", "type": "uint256" }],
    "stateMutability": "view",
    "type": "function"
  }
]
Key takeaway
Always pair the ABI with the correct deployed address for the network you are connected to. A mismatch leads to call or decode failures.
Practical checks & example
  • Confirm ABI version matches compiled contract. If function signatures changed, update the ABI.
  • Confirm the deployed address is on the same network as your provider — local networks and testnets differ.
  • Test a simple read call like get() to validate ABI and address before sending transactions.
Analogy
Think of the ABI as the API documentation and the address as the URL endpoint. You need both to make a correct request.
Common mistake
Using an ABI from a different contract version or using an address deployed to a different network causes function not found or call revert errors.

screens.title: Providers and Signers
screens.narratorSegment: A provider is the interface your frontend uses to send JSON-RPC requests to an Ethereum node. A signer is the entity that can authorize and sign transactions on behalf of a user. Browser wallets like MetaMask inject an EIP-1193 compatible provider into window. ethereum and expose a signer when the user connects. Remote services such as Infura or Alchemy give you read-only access via a provider, but they cannot sign transactions for a user. Practically, this means you use a provider alone for view or pure calls, and you need a signer for any state-changing function. A concrete pattern: instantiate an ethers provider with window. ethereum, then call provider. getSigner() to obtain a signer and create a contract instance that can send transactions. A common misconception is that any provider can sign; only a provider backed by a wallet with private keys can. Finally, ensure you detect when window. ethereum is absent and instruct users to install a wallet. Good UX also shows the connected account and network to avoid surprises when transactions are sent. Providers and Signers means use a provider for reading blockchain state; use a signer, from a connected wallet, to sign transactions and modify state.. In practical terms, how metamask, infura, and a signer enable reads and writes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Provider vs Signer
keyIdea.text: Use a provider for reading blockchain state; use a signer, from a connected wallet, to sign transactions and modify state.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Provider & Signer
Architecture
Provider connects to nodes. Signer holds authority to sign transactions via wallet.
Example code pattern
if (window.ethereum) {
  const provider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
  const signer = await provider.getSigner();
  const contract = new ethers.Contract(contractAddress, contractABI, signer);
} else {
  // Prompt user to install MetaMask
}
Note: Remote providers like Infura are useful for reads and backend tasks, but cannot sign transactions for end users. Browser wallets provide both the provider and the signer when the user connects.
Checks & UX
  • Show connected account address and current network to the user.
  • Detect provider absence and advise wallet installation rather than failing silently.
  • Guard transaction paths with a connected signer and clear confirmation prompts.
Misconception
Not every provider can sign. You cannot send transactions without a signer that holds the user's keys — typically provided by the wallet.

screens.title: Read-only Calls with Ethers.js
screens.narratorSegment: Read-only calls are the simplest interactions: they do not modify blockchain state and therefore do not cost gas. In Ethers. js you call view or pure functions via the contract instance created with a provider or signer. A concrete example from the SimpleStorage contract is calling get() to return the stored number. The pattern is to await the contract. get() call and convert the returned BigNumber to a string for display. Remember these calls are still asynchronous because they may query a remote node. A common pitfall is forgetting to await the promise, which results in unresolved promise objects or stale UI. Another pitfall is assuming read calls do not require a provider; you must supply a provider so the query has a node to contact. After calling, always parse or format returned values before updating the UI. Example: fetch the stored data, display it to the user, and provide a refresh action. Closing question: what checks would you add to your UI to let users know a read is in progress and when it has completed? Read-only Calls with Ethers.js means call view/pure functions via the contract and await the response; format results and surface loading state to users.. In practical terms, calling view and pure functions to fetch on-chain data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reads are asynchronous and provider-backed
keyIdea.text: Call view/pure functions via the contract and await the response; format results and surface loading state to users.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Read-only Calls
Example: get stored value
async function getStoredData() {
  try {
    const data = await contract.get();
    console.log('Stored data:', data.toString());
    return data.toString();
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Error getting data:', error);
  }
}
Tip: Show a loading spinner while awaiting the call and catch errors to avoid leaving the user in a blank state.
Supporting points
  • Read calls require a provider to contact a node, though they don’t need a signer.
  • Always await the promise and convert BigNumber values for display.
  • Implement a refresh control so users can re-query the latest on-chain state.
Misconception
Read calls are free, but they are still network operations that can fail; handle errors and latency in the UI.

screens.title: Sending State-modifying Transactions
screens.narratorSegment: State-modifying functions change blockchain state and therefore require a signed transaction and payment of gas. When you call a non-view function from your frontend, you must ensure a signer is attached to the contract instance. The typical pattern is to call the function on the contract, obtain the transaction object with a hash, then await the transaction receipt to confirm it was mined. Concrete example: calling set on SimpleStorage — you send the transaction, log the transaction hash, then await tx. wait() to get the receipt and confirm the state change. Important UX: inform the user when the transaction is submitted and when it is confirmed, because mining can take time. A common error is attempting to send a transaction without a signer or forgetting to await tx. wait(), which can leave the interface out of sync. Also handle wallet errors: a user may reject signing, or a gas estimation may fail if the contract logic reverts. Always catch errors and provide meaningful messages rather than raw stack traces. Closing reflection: how will your UI communicate pending transactions and confirmations to users?

keyIdea.title: Transactions need signing and confirmation
keyIdea.text: Send a transaction with a signer, await the receipt, and update your UI after confirmation while handling possible failures.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › State-modifying Calls
Example transaction flow
async function setStoredData(newValue) {
  if (!signer) { alert('Connect wallet first'); return; }
  try {
    const tx = await contract.set(newValue);
    console.log('Transaction sent:', tx.hash);
    const receipt = await tx.wait();
    console.log('Transaction confirmed:', receipt);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Error setting data:', error);
  }
}
UX tip: show a pending state after submission and a success state once the receipt arrives. Provide links to the transaction hash when appropriate.
Common errors
  • User rejected transaction: catch specific wallet error codes and inform the user without retrying automatically.
  • UNPREDICTABLE_GAS_LIMIT: gas estimation failed — check contract logic and revert reasons.
  • Insufficient funds: the user’s account must have enough to cover gas.
Key takeaway
Treat transactions as a multi-step asynchronous workflow and surface each step to the user.

screens.title: Read vs Write: Costs, Latency, and UX
screens.narratorSegment: Read-only functions and state-changing transactions differ in cost, latency, and required privileges. Read calls are free and executed by a node without creating a transaction; they are typically fast but still asynchronous. State changes require the user's signature and payment of gas; they produce transactions that must be mined, so latency is higher and confirmations are required. A concrete example: calling get to fetch a stored number returns immediately from a node and you can show the result right away. Calling set requires the user to sign, then the network to mine the transaction before the state is updated. A misconception is treating both as identical — this leads to UI that assumes immediate state change after sending a transaction. Instead, your app should optimistically show a pending state and only update confirmed state after receiving a receipt. Another practical point: use read calls for UI-only data and reserve transactions for deliberate user actions. Closing question: where will you place loading indicators and confirmations in your app to make this distinction clear? Read vs Write: Costs, Latency, and UX means reads are free and fast but asynchronous; writes need signing, cost gas, and require confirmation before the state is truly updated.. In practical terms, how view/pure functions differ from state-changing calls in practice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Reads are free and fast but asynchronous; writes need signing, cost gas, and require confirmation before the state is truly updated.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Read vs Write
Read (view/pure)
No gas, no signature required, executed by a node. Use for displaying state like balances or stored values.
Example: contract.get() returns the stored number. Await the call and format the returned value before rendering.
Write (state-modifying)
Requires a signer and gas. The user must approve the transaction in their wallet and the network must mine it.
Example: contract.set(42) sends a transaction. Show pending status and update the UI after tx.wait() confirms mining.
UX rule of thumb
Treat transaction submission and confirmation as distinct states. Provide clear feedback: requested → submitted (tx hash) → confirmed (receipt). Avoid assuming immediate state changes.

screens.title: Error Handling and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Interacting with contracts from the frontend exposes a small set of predictable error patterns. First, ABI or address mismatch will typically produce function not found or call revert exceptions. Second, asynchronous mistakes — such as forgetting to await promises — lead to unresolved promise objects or stale UI states. Third, gas estimation problems or contract reverts can cause transactions to fail; these require clear messaging explaining why the action failed and how to troubleshoot. Fourth, user rejection is normal: a user can deny signing in the wallet. Catch the specific wallet error codes and inform the user instead of retrying automatically. A concrete handling strategy: wrap calls in try/catch, detect known error codes (like the user rejection code), provide human-friendly messages, and include next steps, such as checking network or account balance. A misconception is exposing raw error stacks to users; instead, log them for debugging and present actionable guidance. Final takeaway: graceful error handling reduces friction and builds user trust in your DApp. Error Handling and Common Mistakes means catch and classify errors — abi/address issues, asynchronous mistakes, gas estimation failures, and user rejections — and present clear, actionable messages.. In practical terms, recognize and respond to typical failures in frontend interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Anticipate and handle errors
keyIdea.text: Catch and classify errors — ABI/address issues, asynchronous mistakes, gas estimation failures, and user rejections — and present clear, actionable messages.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Errors & Mistakes
ABI / Address
Verify ABI matches compiled contract and address is for the expected network. Mismatches produce call revert or function not found errors.
Asynchronous mistakes
Always await promises for reads and transactions; otherwise the UI may show incomplete or incorrect data.
User rejection
Detect and handle user rejection codes (for example, the wallet refusal code). Inform the user rather than retrying automatically.
Practical pattern
  1. Wrap calls in try/catch.

screens.title: Transaction Lifecycle & Gas Estimation
screens.narratorSegment: A transaction lifecycle has clear stages your frontend should surface: construction, user signature, submission, mining (confirmation), and post-confirmation update. When constructing a transaction, the wallet or library often estimates gas. If estimation fails, it may return an UNPREDICTABLE_GAS_LIMIT error; handle this by surfacing a diagnostic and suggesting the user review the transaction. After the user signs, the transaction is broadcast with a hash; you should show the hash and an indication that mining is in progress. Waiting for confirmations requires awaiting the receipt. Some UIs show one confirmation as success, others wait for multiple confirmations depending on security needs. Misconception: assuming immediate finality — block confirmations take time and re-orgs, so design for asynchronous confirmation. Key UX: show pending, show hash, then show confirmed once a receipt arrives, and refresh on-chain reads to display the new state reliably. screens.title: Network Mismatch and Environments
screens.narratorSegment: Network mismatch occurs when the frontend's provider is connected to a different network than the one where the contract is deployed. For example, you may deploy a contract to a local Hardhat node or a testnet, but a user’s wallet could be connected to a different chain. This mismatch leads to failed calls or transactions that go to the wrong chain. Practical safeguards include detecting the provider’s chain ID at connection time and comparing it to the expected chain for your contract address. If they differ, inform the user and guide them to switch networks or select the correct network configuration. When developing, keep separate configuration for local, testnet, and production deployments and store the corresponding ABI and address for each environment. screens.title: Security and User Experience Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Security and good UX go hand in hand when interacting with smart contracts. Never ask users for their private keys; rely on browser wallets to manage keys and signing. When requesting a transaction, provide clear descriptions of what the transaction does and any expected costs. For example, if a function is payable or could consume significant gas, indicate that in the confirmation step. Handle user rejection gracefully by catching the wallet-specific error code and offering next steps, rather than retrying automatically. Log detailed errors for developers but surface concise, actionable messages to users. Another practical tip is to refresh relevant read-only data only after a transaction has been confirmed, avoiding inconsistent displays. A misconception is thinking that more prompts equal safer UX — extra prompts can lead to prompt fatigue. Instead, make each prompt informative and necessary. Closing reflection: how will your app balance security messaging with a streamlined user flow so users are informed without overwhelmed? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll learn the essential plumbing that lets a JavaScript frontend talk to a Solidity smart contract. You will understand two fundamental pieces of information — the ABI, which describes a contract’s public interface, and the contract address, which locates a deployed instance on the chain. We’ll also cover how a Web3 provider, such as a browser wallet or a remote node service, becomes the bridge between your app and Ethereum. You will see concrete examples using Ethers. js to perform read-only calls that don’t cost gas and to send signed transactions that modify state. Along the way, we’ll highlight common pitfalls: ABI mismatches, network mismatch, and user-rejected transactions, and why proper error handling matters for user trust. By the end you’ll be able to wire up a simple DApp, call a getter, and submit a transaction securely via the user’s wallet. Think about a minimal counter or storage contract — the patterns we cover will apply directly when you build your own frontend to interact with deployed contracts.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify the ABI and contract address necessary for frontend interactions, configure a Web3 provider so your DApp can send requests, call read-only functions to fetch on-chain data, and construct signed transactions to modify state. Each objective combines a practical skill with why it matters. For example, knowing where the contract lives on the chain and having its ABI ensures your frontend encodes calls correctly and decodes results reliably. Configuring a provider matters because it defines whether you can only read data or also sign transactions on behalf of the user. Calling view or pure functions lets you show live on-chain information without costing gas, while constructing transactions requires careful handling of gas estimation and user approval. Finally, you will learn common issues such as network mismatches and user rejections, and how to handle them gracefully. These competencies let you build a responsive, trustworthy DApp experience and avoid common user confusion during wallet interactions.

These objectives translate into concrete front-end practices. First, always bundle or load the exact ABI that matches your deployed contract; a mismatch will lead to call failures or 'function not found' errors. Second, detect and surface the connected network to prevent users from sending transactions to the wrong chain. Third, treat every state-changing operation as an asynchronous workflow: prompt the user, send the signed transaction, wait for a receipt, then update the UI. Fourth, provide clear error messages for common issues such as user rejection, gas estimation failures, or insufficient funds. For example, when using Ethers. js, you will instantiate a contract with a provider for read-only access and with a signer for transactions. Practicing these patterns ensures your DApp is reliable, transparent, and respectful of user control over signing transactions.

The ABI, or Application Binary Interface, is a JSON array that describes a smart contract's public interface: its functions, events, state variables, argument types, and return types. The contract address is a unique on-chain identifier created when a contract is deployed. Together they let your frontend encode the binary payload for a function call and target a specific contract instance on a given network. A concrete example: a compiled SimpleStorage contract exposes a get function and a set function. Your frontend needs the ABI to call get and decode the returned number. It also needs the contract's deployed address so the Ethereum nodes know which contract to execute. A frequent misconception is thinking the ABI alone is sufficient; without the address the ABI has no target, and without the ABI the frontend cannot package calls correctly. Key practical checks include ensuring the ABI version matches the deployed bytecode and that you are using the address for the same network as the provider. Final takeaway: ABI describes how to talk, address tells you where to speak. Ask yourself: do I have both the exact ABI and the correct deployed address before attempting calls?

A provider is the interface your frontend uses to send JSON-RPC requests to an Ethereum node. A signer is the entity that can authorize and sign transactions on behalf of a user. Browser wallets like MetaMask inject an EIP-1193 compatible provider into window. ethereum and expose a signer when the user connects. Remote services such as Infura or Alchemy give you read-only access via a provider, but they cannot sign transactions for a user. Practically, this means you use a provider alone for view or pure calls, and you need a signer for any state-changing function. A concrete pattern: instantiate an ethers provider with window. ethereum, then call provider. getSigner() to obtain a signer and create a contract instance that can send transactions. A common misconception is that any provider can sign; only a provider backed by a wallet with private keys can. Finally, ensure you detect when window. ethereum is absent and instruct users to install a wallet. Good UX also shows the connected account and network to avoid surprises when transactions are sent. Providers and Signers means use a provider for reading blockchain state; use a signer, from a connected wallet, to sign transactions and modify state.. In practical terms, how metamask, infura, and a signer enable reads and writes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Read-only calls are the simplest interactions: they do not modify blockchain state and therefore do not cost gas. In Ethers. js you call view or pure functions via the contract instance created with a provider or signer. A concrete example from the SimpleStorage contract is calling get() to return the stored number. The pattern is to await the contract. get() call and convert the returned BigNumber to a string for display. Remember these calls are still asynchronous because they may query a remote node. A common pitfall is forgetting to await the promise, which results in unresolved promise objects or stale UI. Another pitfall is assuming read calls do not require a provider; you must supply a provider so the query has a node to contact. After calling, always parse or format returned values before updating the UI. Example: fetch the stored data, display it to the user, and provide a refresh action. Closing question: what checks would you add to your UI to let users know a read is in progress and when it has completed? Read-only Calls with Ethers.js means call view/pure functions via the contract and await the response; format results and surface loading state to users.. In practical terms, calling view and pure functions to fetch on-chain data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

State-modifying functions change blockchain state and therefore require a signed transaction and payment of gas. When you call a non-view function from your frontend, you must ensure a signer is attached to the contract instance. The typical pattern is to call the function on the contract, obtain the transaction object with a hash, then await the transaction receipt to confirm it was mined. Concrete example: calling set on SimpleStorage — you send the transaction, log the transaction hash, then await tx. wait() to get the receipt and confirm the state change. Important UX: inform the user when the transaction is submitted and when it is confirmed, because mining can take time. A common error is attempting to send a transaction without a signer or forgetting to await tx. wait(), which can leave the interface out of sync. Also handle wallet errors: a user may reject signing, or a gas estimation may fail if the contract logic reverts. Always catch errors and provide meaningful messages rather than raw stack traces. Closing reflection: how will your UI communicate pending transactions and confirmations to users?

Read-only functions and state-changing transactions differ in cost, latency, and required privileges. Read calls are free and executed by a node without creating a transaction; they are typically fast but still asynchronous. State changes require the user's signature and payment of gas; they produce transactions that must be mined, so latency is higher and confirmations are required. A concrete example: calling get to fetch a stored number returns immediately from a node and you can show the result right away. Calling set requires the user to sign, then the network to mine the transaction before the state is updated. A misconception is treating both as identical — this leads to UI that assumes immediate state change after sending a transaction. Instead, your app should optimistically show a pending state and only update confirmed state after receiving a receipt. Another practical point: use read calls for UI-only data and reserve transactions for deliberate user actions. Closing question: where will you place loading indicators and confirmations in your app to make this distinction clear? Read vs Write: Costs, Latency, and UX means reads are free and fast but asynchronous; writes need signing, cost gas, and require confirmation before the state is truly updated.. In practical terms, how view/pure functions differ from state-changing calls in practice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Interacting with contracts from the frontend exposes a small set of predictable error patterns. First, ABI or address mismatch will typically produce function not found or call revert exceptions. Second, asynchronous mistakes — such as forgetting to await promises — lead to unresolved promise objects or stale UI states. Third, gas estimation problems or contract reverts can cause transactions to fail; these require clear messaging explaining why the action failed and how to troubleshoot. Fourth, user rejection is normal: a user can deny signing in the wallet. Catch the specific wallet error codes and inform the user instead of retrying automatically. A concrete handling strategy: wrap calls in try/catch, detect known error codes (like the user rejection code), provide human-friendly messages, and include next steps, such as checking network or account balance. A misconception is exposing raw error stacks to users; instead, log them for debugging and present actionable guidance. Final takeaway: graceful error handling reduces friction and builds user trust in your DApp. Error Handling and Common Mistakes means catch and classify errors — abi/address issues, asynchronous mistakes, gas estimation failures, and user rejections — and present clear, actionable messages.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Network mismatch occurs when the frontend's provider is connected to a different network than the one where the contract is deployed.
